file_verdicts.summary: Standard AUR package with proper checksums and clean build process

audits.body:
Cloning https://aur.archlinux.org/xsnow.git... Cloned xsnow Analyzing xsnow AUR package with openrouter/free Performing initial audit of PKGBUILD to ensure that we can safely run `makepkg` LLM auditresponse for PKGBUILD: SAFE
The PKGBUILD defines a single source URL pointing to the official upstream downloads host (https://www.ratrabbit.nl/downloads/xsnow/xsnow-3.9.0.tar.gz) with a declared b2sums checksum for verification. This URL matches the project URL in the pkgurl field, indicating it is the package's own declared upstream source. The checksum is provided rather than SKIPped, which is an even stronger security posture. There is no pkgver() function defined in this PKGBUILD, so no additional code execution occurs during sourcing beyond the standard parsing of variables. The source array references only the upstream archive, with no command substitution or dynamic URL generation that could redirect downloads to unexpected hosts. The build() and package() functions contain only standard compilation and installation steps (configure, make, install of binaries and data files into $pkgdir). These are conventional AUR/packaging practices and do not exhibit any signs of malicious behavior such as network exfiltration, obfuscated commands, or execution of untrusted code.

This PKGBUILD is a standard, clean Arch Linux package build script for xsnow version 3.9.0. It fetches the source tarball from the official upstream website (ratrabbit.nl) with a proper BLAKE2b checksum for integrity verification. The build process uses the conventional `./configure && make` workflow, and the package() function installs the compiled binary, desktop entry, appdata metadata, icon, and man page into appropriate locations under $pkgdir. No suspicious network requests, obfuscated code, dangerous commands (eval, base64, curl/wget in unexpected contexts), or unexpected file operations are present. The package follows standard AUR packaging practices and shows no signs of supply-chain compromise or injected malicious code.
